summary: Defines RSVP-TE signaling extensions to move a connection between management plane control and GMPLS control plane without disturbing the traffic. This lets permanent connections become soft permanent ones and back. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: You switch who steers a bus from a manager to a driver without stopping the bus or bothering the passengers.

subtitle: How an RSVP-TE signaling flag moves an existing connection between management-system control and GMPLS control without touching traffic.

tldr.problem: Transport networks can have connections owned by a management system (permanent) or by a GMPLS control plane (soft permanent). Operators need to switch ownership of a live connection without disturbing the traffic on it.
tldr.mechanism: A new Handover (H) bit in the RSVP-TE ADMIN_STATUS object marks special Path and Resv exchanges that move ownership of a label switched path while leaving data plane state alone. A new error code reports failures and ownership rolls back.
tldr.outcome: A path can be handed from the management plane to the control plane, and back, with defined behavior for failures and restarts. All nodes on the path must support the extension.

today: RFC 5852 is a Proposed Standard from April 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the Handover procedure for GMPLS RSVP-TE.

sections.title: Handing Over Connection Ownership
sections.content:
In a traditional transport network, a Network Management System (NMS) in the Management Plane (MP) owns the data plane connections between endpoints and handles their setup, teardown and maintenance. When a GMPLS Control Plane (CP) is added to a network already in service, there must be a way to hand a connection from the MP to the CP in a controlled way.

The abstract calls connections owned by the CP Soft Permanent Connections (SPC) and those owned by the management system Permanent Connections (PC). RFC 5493 sets the requirement for converting between them. This RFC extends GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling (RFC 3471, RFC 3473) to do so, a transfer it calls a Handover.

A basic premise is that Handover procedures must never impact user data on LSPs already established in the data plane. MP-to-CP Handover is a mandatory requirement. CP-to-MP Handover is described as a nice-to-have, an emergency procedure to disable the CP and take manual control of the LSP.
sections.eli5: A connection can be run by a manager or by an automatic system. This memo says how to swap who is in charge without interrupting the people using it.

sections.title: MP-to-CP Handover
sections.content:
The procedure changes only the ADMIN_STATUS object, with a new H bit. Message flow for LSP setup and deletion is left unmodified. The operator tells the ingress node to hand over an LSP and supplies its exact path, including resources and labels.

The ingress MUST check that no Path state exists and that data plane state does exist. It then sends a Path message with the H bit and the R bit set, carrying an ERO with Label subobjects, and starts an Expiration timer that SHOULD be configurable per LSP with a default of 30 seconds.

Each LSR that receives the Path message with the H bit set checks for matching state. A refresh is treated normally, a clash with H-clear state is an error, and missing data plane state is an error or race. If matching data plane state is found, the LSR MUST save the Path state with the H bit and forward the message, and it MUST retain any MP state at that point. The egress answers with a Resv carrying the H bit.

When the ingress receives that Resv while the timer runs, it cancels the timer, SHOULD tell the operator the first stage is done, and sends an unchanged Path message with the H bit clear. LSRs SHOULD release their MP state when they see it. When the ingress gets a Resv with the H bit clear, the Handover is complete.
sections.eli5: The first person sends a note down the line saying, "We are about to change drivers." Everyone checks the bus is really there and answers. A second note says the change is done, and the old manager lets go.

sections.title: When MP-to-CP Handover Fails
sections.content:
Two failures can occur, a Path failure or a Resv failure, each caused by either a data plane failure or a communication failure. In every case LSP ownership MUST be rolled back immediately to what it was before the Handover.

If a node hits an error on the Path message, it MUST answer with a PathErr and abort. The PathErr SHOULD have the Path_State_Removed flag set, and the data plane resources MUST NOT be impacted. A node that sees a PathTear while holding Path state with the H bit set MUST remove the Path state, MUST NOT change data plane state, and MUST return ownership to the MP.

When messages are lost, the Expiration timer ends the attempt. With reliable delivery (RFC 2961) the sender retries first. Without it, the ingress sends a PathTear when the timer expires.

For node restarts with graceful restart, the RFC describes three cases. With a finite Restart Time, the neighbor tears down the LSP if the restarting node does not recover, but does not release data plane resources because the H bit is set. With an infinite Restart Time, a recovery timer decides. In the third case the ingress re-sends the Path message with the H bit set, and the neighbor either resumes or aborts according to local policy, never modifying the data plane.
sections.eli5: If anything goes wrong during the swap, the old manager takes the wheel back at once. The bus never stops, and the setup is cleaned up.

sections.title: CP-to-MP Handover
sections.content:
Going the other way, the control plane gives up its LSP and the management plane takes over. The procedure MUST delete the RSVP-TE session information and MUST NOT affect the cross-connected resources. It is a standard LSP deletion as in RFC 3473, started at the ingress by an MP entity.

The ingress MUST send a Path message with the Handover and Reflect bits set. Transit LSRs forward it and nodes store the H bit in their Path and Resv state. After the ingress receives the Resv, it MUST send a PathTear. Downstream nodes processing a PathTear that follows an H-bit Path message MUST NOT remove any data plane state.

Failures must not remove data plane state either. While the H bit is set, a node MUST NOT send a PathTear on failure and reports upstream with a PathErr instead. Only the ingress can send a PathTear, and only as a step in these procedures. If a PathTear is lost and the LSP is not under MP control after the Expiration timer elapses, the RFC asks for manual intervention by the operator.
sections.eli5: To give the steering back, a note goes along the line saying "tear down the automatic paperwork but leave the bus alone." Only the front of the line is allowed to cancel the paperwork.

sections.title: Handover With Minimal Information
sections.content:
The ERO need not carry the full path. The full ERO method and the partial or no-ERO method are not mutually exclusive, and support of both is required.

With minimal information, the ingress needs the outgoing interface ID, the upstream and downstream labels of that interface, and the egress node ID. The Path message carries a LABEL_SET object and an UPSTREAM_LABEL object with those labels, and MUST include the ADMIN_STATUS object with the H bit set. Each node on the path extracts the incoming interface and labels, looks up its data plane cross-connection table to find the next hop's outgoing interface and labels, and builds the next outgoing Path message from those values.

Repeating this at every transit node lets the Handover Path message follow the LSP that already exists in the data plane. The ERO MAY be included as an optional object and used to check resource consistency at port or label level.
sections.eli5: If the first person only knows the first stretch of road, each stop along the way looks up the next stretch in its own map, until the note reaches the end.

sections.title: The H Bit and the Error Code
sections.content:
The RFC adds no changes to the RSVP message composition. It changes two objects. The H bit is new in the ADMIN_STATUS object defined in RFC 3473, and it is bit number 25 (hex value 0x00000040). IANA has allocated it.

It also adds a new Error Code to the ERROR_SPEC object (from RFC 2205): Handover Procedure Failure, value 35. Failures are signaled by a PathErr upstream and PathTear messages downstream, and the PathErr carries the error. Two Error Value sub-codes are defined: 1 for a cross-connection mismatch and 2 for any other failure. On such a failure, ownership stays where it was before the Handover and no traffic hit occurs.
sections.eli5: There is one new flag that means "this is only a paperwork change." There is also a new kind of error message that says the swap failed.

sections.title: Compatibility
sections.content: For Handover to work, all nodes along the path MUST support this extension. This is an administrative requirement rather than something enforced at the protocol level. Nodes that do not support it simply propagate the H bit without setting local state, and that may impact data traffic during the Handover.
sections.eli5: Everyone along the line has to know the new rules. If someone does not, they just pass the note along without understanding it, and that could bump the passengers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures rely entirely on RSVP-TE messages and mechanisms. The H bit tells the receiver that no data plane operations follow from this signaling, which limits setup and teardown messages to the control plane.

However, Handover lets the control plane take an LSP out of the management plane's control. The RFC says this could cause considerable disruption and could introduce a new security concern, so GMPLS security techniques become more important. It refers readers to RFC 3473 for RSVP-TE security.
sections.eli5: Because the swap lets one system take charge from another, it is important to make sure only the right people can ask for it.
